opus-5.5.text:
I think individual talent matters a lot, but it's not sufficient by itself. In my experience leading research teams, a group of very smart people doesn't automatically become a great team. Sometimes it's the opposite. If everyone is brilliant but everyone wants to pursue their own idea, you end up with ten small projects instead of one big thing. In AI today, especially with large-scale efforts like foundation models, the problems are too big for any one person. You need people who are willing to align on a shared goal, and sometimes put their own idea aside to make the collective project succeed.

So for me the question isn't really "smart versus less smart." It's whether the team has a common vision and the right culture. Do people trust each other? Are they willing to do the unglamorous work, like data cleaning, infrastructure, evaluation? Those things often decide whether a project works, and they're not always what the most individually brilliant people want to do.

That said, I don't want to downplay talent. At the frontier, a few exceptional people can change the direction of the whole team. They see things others don't, or they make the key technical decision that saves months. So what I look for is a combination: strong people, but people who are also humble, collaborative, and care about the outcome more than the credit. If you get that combination, the team can be much greater than the sum of its parts. If you only optimize for individual brilliance, you may get a lot of friction and not much output.

And one more thing: the leader's role is important here. Part of my job is to make the goal clear enough that smart people can push in the same direction instead of in different ones. When that works, it's really powerful.

r001.rationale: The response discusses aligning around a shared goal and avoiding friction, but does not identify communication overhead as a cost of bringing people together.

r002.rationale: It asks whether teammates trust each other and says a strong team can be greater than the sum of its parts, but does not clearly present mutual trust as necessary for that outcome.

r003.rationale: It mentions different kinds of work, such as data cleaning and infrastructure, but does not favor teams with complementary capabilities over teams whose members serve the same role.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I've thought about a lot, because I've been in both kinds of teams. I'll give you my honest answer: a team of very smart people doesn't automatically win. It's not even close to automatic.

When I was starting out as a researcher, I believed talent was everything. If you put the smartest people in a room, the best result would come out. But what I actually observed, over many years and many teams, is something different. Very smart people often have very strong opinions, and they've been rewarded their whole lives for being right. So when you put ten of them together, a lot of energy goes into proving who is right, rather than into building the thing. Each person wants to own the most interesting problem. Nobody wants to do the unglamorous work, the data cleaning, the infrastructure, the evaluation pipeline. And in our field, that unglamorous work is often where the result actually comes from.

So what I've learned to look for is not just how smart someone is, but whether they can be smart together. Can they listen? Can they let go of their idea when someone else has a better one? Can they be excited about the team winning rather than themselves winning? A team where people have slightly less raw brilliance but genuinely trust each other and move in one direction, that team will often beat the all-star team. I've seen it happen many times.

That said, I don't want to romanticize it. There are problems where you really do need someone exceptional. Some breakthroughs come from one person who sees something nobody else sees. Talent is not optional. But I think of it as a threshold. Above a certain level, additional individual brilliance gives you less and less, and the thing that determines success becomes culture. Whether people feel safe to say "I was wrong." Whether the leader is actually leading or just collecting famous names.

So if you asked me to build a team today, I would want everyone to be good, clearly good, but I would spend most of my attention on how they work together, and on whether they share the same goal. The smartest team I was ever on did not produce the best work I've been part of. The team that cared the most about each other did.

r001.rationale: The response says energy can be spent proving who is right instead of building, but it does not clearly identify communication overhead as a cost of bringing people together in a team.

r002.rationale: It says a team that genuinely trusts each other and moves in one direction can beat a team with greater individual brilliance, and emphasizes trust and shared goals as central to success.

r003.rationale: It mentions neglected tasks such as data cleaning and infrastructure, but does not favor teams whose members bring complementary capabilities over teams whose members serve the same role.

astra-6.text:
I think individual ability matters a lot, but it’s not enough to predict how successful a team will be. You also have to ask whether those people can work toward a shared goal, communicate clearly, and learn from one another.

If everyone is exceptionally smart but each person wants to pursue their own direction, the team can spend a lot of energy without making much progress. A team whose members are less individually outstanding may accomplish more because their strengths complement each other and they work together well.

So I wouldn’t frame it as a choice between talent and teamwork. Ideally, you want both. When you bring in a very strong person, the question is also: does this person help the people around them become more effective? That’s what makes individual talent translate into team success.

r001.rationale: The response says teams should communicate clearly, but does not identify communication overhead as a cost that reduces the benefits of teamwork.

r002.rationale: The response discusses working together well, but does not present mutual trust as necessary for team success.

r003.rationale: The response says complementary strengths can help a team, but does not compare this with teams whose members all serve the same role.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think individual intelligence alone tells you how successful a team will be. It matters, of course, but so does whether those people can work toward the same goal, communicate clearly, and learn from one another.

You can put exceptionally smart people together, but if everyone wants to prove that their idea is best, the team may struggle to make progress. A team whose members are less individually outstanding can accomplish more if their strengths complement each other and they trust one another enough to challenge ideas and admit mistakes.

So I would look at how the team works together. Does a disagreement help them find a better answer? Can they make a decision and execute it together? Ideally, you want exceptional people who also make the people around them more effective.

r001.rationale: The response recommends clear communication but does not identify communication overhead as a cost that reduces the benefits of teamwork.

r002.rationale: It links trust to challenging ideas and admitting mistakes, but does not say that mutual trust is necessary for the team to achieve more than the sum of individual contributions.

r003.rationale: It says a team can accomplish more when members’ strengths complement each other, favoring complementary capabilities.
